_readme: Authored extensions to the existing library datasets (say/ hanbang/ ask/ term/) plus four new clusters, merged by build-kbeauty-pages.cjs alongside the originals. Shapes match the files they extend. Romanisations follow Revised Romanization; respellings are approximate English guides, not IPA.

brands.name: d'Alba
brands.meaning: From Alba, the Italian region famed for white truffles — the brand's signature ingredient.

brands.name: Heimish
brands.meaning: From the Yiddish-derived word heimish, meaning homely or cosy.

brands.name: I'm From
brands.meaning: English phrase — the brand names the Korean region each hero ingredient comes from.

brands.name: rom&nd
brands.meaning: Coined; read as 'romand', a contraction the brand leaves deliberately open.

brands.name: CLIO
brands.meaning: From Clio, the Greek muse of history.

brands.name: peripera
brands.meaning: Coined brand name with no literal Korean meaning.

brands.name: Goodal
brands.meaning: Coined; commonly read as a blend of 'good' and the Korean 달 (dal, moon).

brands.name: Banila Co
brands.meaning: From vanilla — Korean renders the English word as 바닐라.

brands.name: TONYMOLY
brands.meaning: Coined; the Korean spelling ends in -mori rather than -moly.

brands.name: Hanyul
brands.meaning: 한 (han, Korean/one) + 율 (yul, rhythm or law) — roughly 'the Korean rhythm'.

brands.name: VT Cosmetics
brands.meaning: Initials; Koreans read the letters as 브이티.

brands.name: Axis-Y
brands.meaning: English coinage referencing the y-axis.

brands.name: Hanskin
brands.meaning: 한 (han, Korean) + skin.

brands.name: Aestura
brands.meaning: Coined; note the Korean reads closer to 'estra' than to 'aestura'.

brands.name: Illiyoon
brands.meaning: Coined brand name.

brands.name: Dr.G
brands.meaning: Doctor G — Koreans say 닥터지, running the two together.

brands.name: Celimax
brands.meaning: Coined, from cell + max.

brands.name: SIORIS
brands.meaning: Coined brand name.

brands.name: Aromatica
brands.meaning: From aromatic — the brand began in aromatherapy.

brands.name: KAHI
brands.meaning: Coined brand name.

brands.name: A'PIEU
brands.meaning: Coined; the Korean 어퓨 is closer to 'uh-pyu' than to 'a-pew'.

brands.name: The Saem
brands.meaning: 샘 (saem) is Korean for spring or fountain.

brands.name: eSpoir
brands.meaning: From the French espoir, meaning hope.

brands.name: hince
brands.meaning: Coined; one syllable in Korean, not two.

brands.name: AMUSE
brands.meaning: English word amuse.

ingredients.name: Adenosine
ingredients.meaning: Korea's most-used notified wrinkle-improvement active.

ingredients.name: Bifida Ferment Lysate
ingredients.meaning: 발효 (balhyo) means fermentation — the word that anchors an entire K-beauty category.

ingredients.name: Birch Sap
ingredients.meaning: 자작나무 is birch tree, 수액 is sap.

ingredients.name: Camellia Oil
ingredients.meaning: 동백 (dongbaek) is the camellia flower, long associated with Jeju.

ingredients.name: Yuja
ingredients.meaning: The Korean citron — the same fruit as Japanese yuzu, called yuja in Korea.

ingredients.name: Pomegranate
ingredients.meaning: Note the pronunciation shift: 석류 is written seok-ryu but said seong-nyu.

ingredients.name: Mung Bean
ingredients.meaning: Ground nokdu is one of Korea's oldest cleansing traditions.

ingredients.name: Black Ginseng
ingredients.meaning: 흑 (heuk) means black — ginseng steamed and dried through repeated cycles.

ingredients.name: Pearl Extract
ingredients.meaning: 진주 is pearl; 추출물 means extract, a word worth knowing on any label.

ingredients.name: Royal Jelly
ingredients.meaning: Loanword from English.

ingredients.name: Bamboo Sap
ingredients.meaning: 대나무 is bamboo.

ingredients.name: Aloe Vera
ingredients.meaning: Three syllables in Korean, not two.

ingredients.name: Tea Tree
ingredients.meaning: Loanword; ubiquitous on Korean blemish-care packaging.

ingredients.name: Collagen
ingredients.meaning: Loanword — note the hard g, unlike English.

ingredients.name: Caffeine
ingredients.meaning: Loanword; the same word Koreans use for coffee's caffeine.

ingredients.name: Retinal
ingredients.meaning: Distinct from 레티놀 (retinol) — one syllable's difference, a real difference in strength.

ingredients.name: Exosome
ingredients.meaning: Loanword; the most-hyped term in Korean clinic skincare.

ingredients.name: Ectoin
ingredients.meaning: Loanword.

ingredients.name: Licorice Root
ingredients.meaning: 감초 is also a Korean idiom for someone who turns up in everything — it appears in nearly every herbal remedy.

ingredients.name: Fermented Soybean
ingredients.meaning: 대두 is soybean; the same fermentation tradition behind doenjang.

term.def: Literally 'inner dryness' — skin that is oily on the surface yet tight and dehydrated underneath. One of the most useful Korean skincare concepts, and the reason oily skin still needs hydration.
Literally 'water shine' — the wet-looking, luminous finish that Korean makeup and skincare aim for. The opposite of a matte finish, and the aesthetic ancestor of glass skin.
The particular quality of skin that feels moist, supple and comfortable rather than greasy. Korean product copy uses it constantly; English has no single equivalent.
Soothing or calming. The word on every cica product in Korea, and the single most useful Korean term to recognise if your skin reacts easily.
Dead surface skin. Korean exfoliating products are almost always labelled with this word, whether they use acids, enzymes or a peeling gel.
Pores. Appears on pore-focused toners, serums and masks — usually paired with 축소 (reduction), a claim about appearance rather than actual pore size.
Elasticity or firmness. The word Korean anti-ageing lines use in place of the wrinkle-focused framing common in Western marketing.

A gel that pills as you rub it, taking loose surface debris with it. The pilling is mostly the gel's own cellulose polymer, not your dead skin — gentle and satisfying, but less exfoliating than it looks.
What Koreans call toner. The naming difference is the source of most Western confusion about Korean routines: 스킨 is a hydrating first step, not an astringent.
An overnight mask applied as the last step of a PM routine, designed to seal everything beneath it. It goes over your moisturiser, not instead of it.
A watery, high-percentage ferment applied immediately after cleansing, before anything else. The category SK-II created and Korean brands made affordable.
A concentrated treatment, typically more potent than a serum and sold in a smaller bottle. The distinction is marketing convention rather than a regulated definition.
A small adhesive dressing that absorbs fluid from an open blemish and, just as usefully, physically stops you picking at it. A Korean pharmacy staple that went global.
The Korean counter-movement to the ten-step routine: fewer, better-chosen products with multiple functions. A response to the excess the export marketing created.
Skin with a soft, warm, glowing finish — less mirror-like than glass skin and more attainable. Korean beauty vocabulary distinguishes several finishes English lumps together as 'glowy'.
The Korean shorthand for soft, poreless-looking, unlined skin — a compliment and a marketing target in equal measure.
Culturing an ingredient with micro-organisms before use. Korea's food culture ran on fermentation long before its cosmetics did, and 발효 on a label signals that lineage.
Korea's regulatory tier between ordinary cosmetics and drugs. Products in it may make reviewed claims such as brightening, wrinkle improvement or UV protection.
Sunscreen in a solid twist-up tube. Convenient for reapplication over makeup, and very easy to under-apply — it needs far more passes than feel sufficient.
A pre-soaked pad delivering a measured dose of toner or mild exfoliant. One of Korea's most successful format inventions, and easy to over-use if it contains acids.
A cleanser formulated near skin's own slightly acidic surface rather than alkaline. The Korean shift away from squeaky-clean foaming washes started here.

A temporary increase in breakouts when starting a turnover-accelerating active. Only retinoids and exfoliating acids can cause it, only where you already break out, and only for about four to six weeks.
The outermost layer of skin and the lipids between its cells, which hold water in and irritants out. Nearly every modern Korean skincare trend is, underneath, about protecting it.
The normal, thread-like structure that channels oil out of a pore. Frequently mistaken for a blackhead, and impossible to remove permanently — it refills because it is meant to.
The hydrated, softly reflective finish Korean routines aim for, as opposed to the matte finish that dominated Western makeup for decades.
Korea's dominant health-and-beauty retail chain. Its shelves are the closest thing to a live ranking of what Korea is actually buying, which is why its sales are watched as a trend indicator.
Shorthand for Centella asiatica, the soothing botanical behind an entire Korean product category. Named for the centella-derived compounds associated with calming irritated-looking skin.

ask.q: How many steps should a Korean skincare routine have?
ask.answer: As few as three: cleanser, moisturiser and sunscreen. The ten-step routine was a Western marketing frame rather than a Korean rule — most Koreans use a handful of products daily and add extras occasionally.
ask.detail: The genuinely useful idea inside the marketing is layering thin hydration rather than relying on one heavy cream, plus treating sunscreen as non-negotiable. The count itself is arbitrary.
ask.koreaNote: The Korean counter-movement is called 스킵케어 (skip-care) — fewer, better-chosen, multi-purpose products.

ask.answer: 속건조 describes skin that looks and feels oily on the surface while being tight and dehydrated underneath. It is why oily skin still needs hydration, and why stripping it makes things worse.
ask.detail: The fix is humectants and barrier support rather than more oil control. Skin that is dehydrated often produces more oil to compensate, which is how the cycle sustains itself.
ask.koreaNote: The concept is standard vocabulary in Korean skincare and has no neat English equivalent — 'dehydrated oily skin' is the closest.

ask.answer: Because Korea approves modern UV filters — Uvinul A Plus, Tinosorb S and M among them — that give strong UVA protection in light, non-greasy textures. Some markets, notably the US, have not approved them.
ask.detail: It is a regulatory difference, not a chemistry secret. Korea regulates sunscreen as a functional cosmetic with a workable approval path; the US regulates it as an over-the-counter drug, which has made new filters extremely slow to arrive.
ask.koreaNote: Korean sunscreens show both SPF for UVB and a PA rating for UVA.

ask.q: Does Korean skincare work for deeper skin tones?
ask.answer: The skincare does — hydration, barrier support and soothing actives are not tone-specific. The friction points are mineral sunscreens that leave a cast and a colour-cosmetics shade range that has historically been narrow.
ask.detail: For sunscreen, look for organic-filter formulas rather than high-zinc mineral ones, which cast less. Brightening actives such as niacinamide and tranexamic acid are genuinely useful for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, which affects deeper tones more persistently.
ask.koreaNote: Shade ranges have widened considerably since around 2023, driven partly by international demand.

ask.q: How long before Korean skincare shows results?
ask.answer: Hydration shows within days. Texture and breakouts take about four to eight weeks. Pigmentation and fine lines take three months or more. Judging anything earlier than its timeframe is the most common reason people abandon products that were working.
ask.detail: Skin turnover takes roughly a month, and most actives need several cycles to show their effect. Consistency over three months beats intensity over three weeks in almost every category.
ask.koreaNote: Korean routines emphasise steady daily habit over aggressive intervention, which is partly why they suit long timeframes.

ask.q: Can I mix Korean and Western skincare?
ask.answer: Yes. Products do not care where they were made — what matters is the ingredients and the order you apply them. Layer thinnest to thickest, avoid stacking two exfoliating actives, and introduce anything new one at a time.
ask.detail: A common and effective combination is Korean hydration layers and sunscreen with a Western prescription retinoid or a well-formulated vitamin C.
ask.koreaNote: Korean sunscreen is the single most worthwhile swap for most people, because the texture advantage is real and it makes daily use easier.

ask.q: Do I really need to double cleanse?
ask.answer: At night, if you wear sunscreen or makeup — yes. Water-based cleansers cannot break down water-resistant sunscreen, so a single cleanse leaves a film behind. In the morning, one gentle cleanse or just water is plenty.
ask.detail: The first cleanse is oil-based and goes on dry skin to dissolve oil-soluble grime. The second is water-based and removes what is left along with sweat and residue.
ask.koreaNote: 이중세안 (ijung-sean) is the Korean term, and it is treated as routine hygiene rather than an indulgence.

ask.q: Is Korean skincare different for men?
ask.answer: Skin is skin — the actives that work do not change by gender. What differs is context: shaving irritates and mildly exfoliates, male skin tends to be thicker and oilier on average, and men's ranges are usually formulated lighter and unscented.
ask.detail: A workable starting routine is a gentle cleanser, a light moisturiser and sunscreen, adding a soothing product if shaving leaves skin reactive.
ask.koreaNote: Korea has one of the world's highest rates of men's skincare use, and men's ranges are a mainstream category rather than a niche one.

ask.q: How long does Korean skincare last?
ask.answer: Unopened and stored sensibly, most Korean cosmetics are given around three years from the manufacturing date. Once opened, follow the PAO symbol — the little open jar marked 6M or 12M — which is what actually applies.
ask.detail: Vitamin C and retinoid products degrade fastest and should be replaced on schedule regardless of how much is left. A changed colour, smell or texture overrides any printed date.
ask.koreaNote: Korean packaging often shows a manufacturing date marked 제조 rather than an expiry date — a date after 제조 is when it was made.

ask.q: What is a first essence and do I need one?
ask.answer: A first essence is a watery, high-percentage ferment applied straight after cleansing, before anything else. It is a hydration and conditioning step. Pleasant and popular, but genuinely optional.
ask.detail: The category began with SK-II's pitera and Korean brands made it affordable. Evidence for ferment filtrates is emerging rather than strong, so treat it as a nice-feeling conditioning layer.
ask.koreaNote: In Korean it is 퍼스트 에센스, and it sits before rather than instead of your regular essence or serum.

ask.q: What does cica mean in Korean skincare?
ask.answer: Cica is shorthand for Centella asiatica, a botanical used across Korean soothing products. Cica formulas are aimed at the look of redness, irritation and a stressed barrier.
ask.detail: The plant supplies several related compounds — madecassoside and asiaticoside among them — which is why some products list those individually rather than the whole extract.
ask.koreaNote: 시카 (cica) is one of the most recognisable words on Korean packaging, and 진정 (soothing) usually appears alongside it.

ask.q: Can I use vitamin C and retinol together?
ask.answer: Not in the same layer, but easily in the same routine — vitamin C in the morning, retinol at night. That split suits both: vitamin C partners with sunscreen, and retinoids are degraded by light.
ask.detail: The old warning that they neutralise each other is overstated, but they prefer different pH conditions and stacking them raises irritation for no added benefit.
ask.koreaNote: Korean routines separate them naturally, since morning routines are built around sunscreen and evening around treatment.

ask.q: How do you get glass skin?
ask.answer: Hydration layered on damp skin, a healthy barrier, gentle regular exfoliation for smoothness, and daily sunscreen. Glass skin is a lighting effect produced by a smooth, well-hydrated surface — not something a single product delivers.
ask.detail: In practice: a low-pH cleanser, a hydrating toner pressed in while damp, an essence, a light moisturiser, and sunscreen. Exfoliate once or twice a week, no more.
ask.koreaNote: 유리 피부 (yuri-pibu) is an aesthetic ideal in Korea, not a health standard — and it photographs better than it lives.

ask.answer: Korea has prohibited animal testing for cosmetics, with limited exceptions, so most Korean brands can credibly carry cruelty-free positioning. The complication is export: selling into markets that require animal testing can change a brand's status.
ask.detail: Vegan is a separate question from cruelty-free — many Korean formulas contain snail filtrate, propolis, honey or royal jelly, which are animal-derived without involving testing.
ask.koreaNote: Vegan certification marks are increasingly common on Korean packaging, particularly from indie brands.

ask.q: What is a Korean toner pad?
ask.answer: A pre-soaked cotton or embossed pad delivering a measured dose of toner, or of a mild exfoliating or soothing treatment. It removes the guesswork about how much product to use.
ask.detail: The important thing is to read what is on the pad. A hydrating pad can be used daily; an AHA or BHA pad used on the same schedule is one of the most common causes of accidental over-exfoliation.
ask.koreaNote: 토너패드 became one of Korea's biggest format categories in the 2020s, with brands like Abib and Numbuzin leading it.

ask.q: How often should you exfoliate in a Korean routine?
ask.answer: Once or twice a week for most people, up to three times for oily and resilient skin. Frequency matters far more than strength — a mild acid used consistently beats a strong one that forces you to stop.
ask.detail: Never stack two exfoliating acids, and skip exfoliation entirely on nights you use a retinoid. If skin stings with products it used to tolerate, that is the signal to stop for two to four weeks.
ask.koreaNote: Korean peeling gels feel like they exfoliate more than they do — much of the pilling is the gel's own polymer.

ask.q: What is the difference between essence, serum and ampoule?
ask.answer: Essence is the lightest and most hydration-focused, serum is more concentrated and targeted, and ampoule is the most concentrated of the three. The boundaries are marketing convention, not regulated definitions.
ask.detail: You do not need all three. Choose by texture and by what the formula actually contains rather than by which word is on the bottle.
ask.koreaNote: In Korean these are 에센스, 세럼 and 앰플 — and Korean brands use the terms more loosely than the tidy hierarchy suggests.

hanbang.name: Mugwort (Ssuk)
hanbang.heritageNote: Mugwort is embedded in Korean culture beyond medicine — it appears in the Dangun foundation myth, in seasonal foods such as ssuk-tteok, and in the traditional practice of mugwort steam bathing. Traditional Korean medical texts record it among the herbs used for warming and soothing applications.
hanbang.modernUse: In modern K-beauty mugwort extract is used in soothing lines aimed at the look of redness and sensitivity, often in essences, masks and cleansing oils. Cosmetic claims centre on the appearance of calmer, more comfortable skin rather than any medical effect.
hanbang.caution: Mugwort is related to ragweed and other Asteraceae plants. If you have a pollen allergy in that family, patch-test before use.

hanbang.name: Peony
hanbang.heritageNote: Peony root is a long-standing ingredient in East Asian herbal tradition and appears in Korean hanbang formulations. It was historically associated with women's tonics and with formulas intended to be restorative.
hanbang.modernUse: Used in hanbang skincare as a botanical extract in brightening and firming-focused lines, particularly in premium ranges that lean on traditional formulation heritage. Claims concern the appearance of tone and radiance.
hanbang.caution: A botanical extract with limited independent cosmetic evidence. Treat efficacy claims as appearance-based.

hanbang.name: Korean Angelica
hanbang.heritageNote: Danggwi is one of the most frequently used herbs in Korean traditional medicine, appearing across many classical formulations. It has a long association with circulation-related and women's health preparations in the hanbang tradition.
hanbang.modernUse: Appears in hanbang cosmetic blends, usually as one botanical among several rather than as a headline active, in lines marketed for radiance and vitality.
hanbang.caution: Some angelica species contain compounds that can increase sun sensitivity. Use sunscreen — which you should be doing regardless.

hanbang.name: Houttuynia (Eoseongcho)
hanbang.heritageNote: Named for its distinctive fishy smell — 어성 means fish smell — houttuynia has a long folk-medicine history in Korea and across East Asia, traditionally used in preparations for skin complaints.
hanbang.modernUse: One of the biggest K-beauty ingredient stories of recent years, driven by brands building entire lines around high-percentage heartleaf extract for blemish-prone and reactive skin.
hanbang.caution: Very well tolerated in general, though as with any botanical, patch-test if your skin reacts easily.

hanbang.name: Sophora Root
hanbang.heritageNote: Gosam, literally 'bitter ginseng', appears in Korean traditional medicine for external preparations. Its bitterness is proverbial, and it was used in washes rather than taken lightly.
hanbang.modernUse: Used in scalp and blemish-focused Korean formulas as a traditional botanical extract, generally in combination with other herbs.
hanbang.caution: Independent cosmetic evidence is limited. Treat as a heritage botanical rather than a proven active.

hanbang.name: Poria (Bokryeong)
hanbang.heritageNote: A fungus that grows on pine roots, poria is a classic component of Korean hanbang formulations and appears in the Donguibogam among preparations associated with balance and calm.
hanbang.modernUse: Used in premium hanbang skincare as part of traditional herbal complexes, often in lines that name their formulation lineage explicitly.
hanbang.caution: Used as one botanical within a blend; there is little standalone cosmetic evidence.

hanbang.name: Schisandra (Omija)
hanbang.heritageNote: Omija means 'five-flavour fruit' — sweet, sour, bitter, pungent and salty at once — and it is drunk as a tea across Korea. It appears in traditional preparations associated with vitality.
hanbang.modernUse: Used in antioxidant-positioned Korean formulas and in hanbang lines, valued for its polyphenol content and its cultural recognisability.
hanbang.caution: A mild antioxidant extract; cosmetic evidence is limited.

hanbang.name: Lotus
hanbang.heritageNote: The lotus carries strong Buddhist symbolism in Korea and appears in temple cuisine and traditional preparations. Its association with purity made it a natural fit for beauty formulations.
hanbang.modernUse: Used in hydrating and soothing hanbang formulas, frequently in temple-inspired or heritage-positioned lines.
hanbang.caution: Primarily a heritage and sensory ingredient. Cosmetic evidence is limited.

hanbang.name: Cnidium (Cheongung)
hanbang.heritageNote: Cheongung is a classic hanbang herb, frequently paired with danggwi in traditional Korean formulations associated with circulation.
hanbang.modernUse: Appears within traditional herbal complexes in premium Korean skincare, especially in lines that reference classical formulations by name.
hanbang.caution: Used as part of a blend; little standalone cosmetic evidence exists.

hanbang.name: Rehmannia (Jihwang)
hanbang.heritageNote: Jihwang is among the most-used roots in Korean traditional medicine and appears in the Donguibogam. Preparation method matters in the tradition — raw, dried and steamed forms are treated as distinct.
hanbang.modernUse: Used in luxury hanbang skincare as part of heritage herbal complexes, particularly in ranges aimed at mature skin.
hanbang.caution: A heritage botanical within blends; independent cosmetic evidence is limited.
